standard.title: Experiment with sound and word patterns
standard.description: identify, reproduce and experiment with rhythmic sound and word patterns in poems, chants, rhymes or songs
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss and imitate sound patterns including alliteration and rhyme in poems, chants and songs (AC9E1LE04). They have not yet reproduced patterns with accuracy or experimented with inventing new rhythmic sound and word patterns.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify, reproduce and experiment with rhythmic sound and word patterns in poems, chants, rhymes and songs.

nodes.label: Identifying rhythmic patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the rhythmic pattern in a poem, chant or rhyme — including where stresses fall and where lines repeat — and describe the pattern.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the rhythmic pattern in a simple poem or chant by marking stressed syllables or describing the pattern of repetition.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and compare rhythmic patterns across multiple poems, chants and songs — noting patterns of stress, repetition and line length — and discuss the effects of different patterns.
wider: Compare the rhythmic patterns of chants from different cultural traditions and discuss how rhythm serves the purpose (ceremony, play, story)
Identify rhythmic patterns in poems with irregular rhythms and discuss the effect of variation
success_criteria: Student can describe the rhythmic pattern of a given poem or chant.
Student can identify where stresses fall or where repetition occurs in the pattern.

nodes.label: Reproducing sound patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can reproduce a rhythmic sound or word pattern from a poem, chant, rhyme or song with accuracy.
nodes.minimum_width: Read or recite a poem or chant maintaining its rhythmic pattern with reasonable accuracy.
nodes.typical_width: Reproduce rhythmic patterns from multiple poems and chants across different forms — rhyming couplets, repetitive refrains, alliterative patterns — maintaining the pattern's key features.
wider: Perform a chant or poem with deliberate variation in volume, pace and emphasis to highlight the rhythmic pattern
Reproduce a rhythmic pattern in a different context — e.g. applying the pattern from one poem to new content

response_modes.reason: Reproducing rhythmic patterns accurately requires repeated practice — the motor and auditory memory involved in maintaining a pattern across performance needs consolidation. Practice across multiple performances is more productive than widening the types of patterns at this stage.

success_criteria: Student can reproduce the key features of a rhythmic pattern — stress, repetition, rhyme — with reasonable accuracy.
Student maintains the pattern across the whole poem or chant, not just the first line.

nodes.label: Experimenting with new patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can experiment with creating their own rhythmic sound and word patterns — inventing new words, changing syllables, substituting sounds — to produce a poem, chant or rhyming sequence.
nodes.minimum_width: Create a short original rhythmic sequence (at least two lines) that uses a deliberate sound or word pattern.
nodes.typical_width: Experiment with syllable manipulation, invented words and sound substitution to create original rhythmic sequences; explore how poets use word sounds to create effects for an audience.
wider: Create a new verse for an existing poem or chant that maintains the original rhythmic pattern
Invent nonsense words using known sound patterns and discuss how sound can create meaning even when words are invented

response_modes.reason: Experimenting with sound patterns benefits from an explicit creative reasoning scaffold — what pattern am I using, what sound effect am I going for, does my line fit the pattern? Making this process visible helps students move from accidental to deliberate sound play.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Invented words and nonsense poetry are genuinely rich for phonological awareness and creative play. Advancing students can explore how sound creates atmosphere and meaning even without semantic content — a vivid and productive direction within Year 2.
success_criteria: Student produces an original rhythmic sequence with an identifiable pattern.
Student can explain what sound or word pattern they used and what effect they were aiming for.
